original_assignment_row.title: El Salvador Prison Deportation - Erik Prince $100 Million Military Contractor Plan
original_assignment_row.description_short: El Salvador Prison Deportation - Erik Prince $100 Million Military Contractor Plan
original_assignment_row.description_medium: Politico reported on April 11, 2025, that Erik Prince pitched the administration a plan for a 10,000-person detention camp and deportations of up to 100,000 people to El Salvador. The report said White House interest was unclear. It described a contractor proposal, not an approved $100 million contract or an operating deportation program.
original_assignment_row.description_long: Donald Trump's administration negotiated with former Blackwater CEO Erik Prince to implement an 'unprecedented prison plan' that would deport '100,000 of the worst criminal offenders' to El Salvador prisons through a $100 million military contractor operation involving 10,000-person detention camps and private aircraft fleets operated by Prince's defense contracting network. The systematic foreign deportation represented Trump's implementation of the most extreme immigration enforcement proposal in American history, using military contractors to transport detained immigrants from U.S. prisons to foreign detention facilities while Prince's company handled logistics for gathering prisoners, processing immigration files, and operating international detention operations. The El Salvador prison plan violated international law and constitutional due process protections by sending U.S. residents to foreign prisons without judicial review, while creating unprecedented privatization of immigration enforcement through military contractors who had previously operated in war zones using violence and weapons against civilian populations. Prince's deportation proposal demonstrated Trump's willingness to outsource core government functions to private military contractors while creating profit opportunities for defense industry allies who saw 'potential profits in mass deportations' through government contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The foreign prison deportation violated sovereignty principles and international human rights law by using military contractors to forcibly transfer detainees to foreign countries without legal protections, judicial oversight, or diplomatic agreements ensuring humane treatment and legal representation for transported individuals. The unprecedented privatization represented what immigration advocates called 'extraordinary militarization' of deportation policy that treated immigration enforcement as military operation requiring private contractors with combat experience rather than law enforcement professionals trained in civil rights protections and due process procedures.

original_assignment_row.title: Disability Rights Rollbacks and ADA Enforcement Elimination - Accommodation Requirements Destruction
original_assignment_row.description_short: Disability Rights Rollbacks and ADA Enforcement Elimination - Accommodation Requirements Destruction
original_assignment_row.description_medium: Disability-rights sources describe Project 2025 proposals that could affect Medicaid support, ADA enforcement and community-based services. They do not establish that the administration abolished ADA accommodations or forced disabled people into institutions, and identify no operative rule or implemented funding cut. Those outcomes remain unsupported.
original_assignment_row.description_long: Donald Trump systematically eliminated disability rights protections by gutting Americans with Disabilities Act enforcement, ending Medicaid funding that enabled community living, and removing 'disparate impact' discrimination protections that had addressed systemic ableism while forcing disabled Americans back into institutional settings through funding cuts and accommodation elimination. The comprehensive disability rights destruction represented Trump's implementation of Project 2025's plan to eliminate federal regulations and programs that supported independent living, with $880 billion in Medicaid cuts that would 'strip coverage from 17 million people' including disabled Americans who relied on federal healthcare for wheelchairs, ventilators, personal care attendants, and community-based services. The ADA rollback included eliminating 'disparate impact' discrimination protections that addressed unintentional but systematic bias against disabled people, while removing federal requirements for businesses, educational institutions, and government agencies to provide reasonable accommodations that ensured equal access and participation. Trump's disability targeting violated constitutional equal protection principles by removing legal tools that disabled Americans used to 'highlight ableism within institutions' and seek redress for discrimination, while Medicaid cuts forced disabled people 'out of their homes and into hospitals and nursing homes' against their will and constitutional rights. The disability rights elimination created what advocates called return to 'earlier, shameful era of isolation, exclusion, and institutionalization' by removing Olmstead protections that affirmed disabled people's right to live in community settings with appropriate supports rather than segregated institutional facilities. The systematic accommodation destruction represented Project 2025's vision of society that abandoned federal responsibility for disability inclusion, transforming disabled Americans from equal citizens with supported rights into vulnerable populations subject to institutional control and social exclusion through elimination of legal protections and community-based services.

original_assignment_row.title: Trump admin freezes billions in childcare, other social services against Democratic states
original_assignment_row.description_short: Trump admin freezes billions in childcare, other social services against Democratic states
original_assignment_row.description_medium: The linked timeline says HHS announced on January 6, 2026, that five states would lose federal support for family assistance, child care and social-service grants. It lists about $7.3 billion for TANF, $2.4 billion for child care and $870 million for social-service grants. Those amounts total roughly $10.6 billion, while the page describes the overall figure as $10 billion; it does not specify duration or effective dates.
original_assignment_row.description_long: On January 6, 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services announced that Minnesota, New York, California, Illinois and Colorado would lose federal funding for three programs, according to the linked timeline. It lists about $7.3 billion for Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, nearly $2.4 billion for the Child Care and Development Fund and about $870 million in social-service grants. The component amounts add to approximately $10.6 billion, although the page rounds the overall total to $10 billion. The report says the administration cited alleged fraud in the states but did not present evidence in the account. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker warned that about 152,000 children could be affected. The source uses “freeze” in its headline and describes the action as cancellation in the text, but provides no agency notice, duration or effective period to clarify whether funds were paused or permanently withdrawn. It also does not establish the legal outcome or subsequent effect on recipients. This entry can record the announced funding action and its stated scope, but needs the underlying HHS notice to resolve the total and characterize the action precisely.

The dispute concerned whether the executive branch could impose a national proof-of-citizenship rule without congressional authorization. original_assignment_row.title: Trump Deploys Supporters as 'Poll Watchers' — Voter Intimidation at the Polls
original_assignment_row.description_short: Trump Deploys Supporters as 'Poll Watchers' — Voter Intimidation at the Polls
original_assignment_row.description_medium: Reuters reported that pro-Trump observers disrupted ballot-counting work during a July 2024 Milwaukee-area primary. Election officials described coordinated objections at several Glendale sites and the central count; police were called, and two observers were told to leave. Reuters did not establish that the Trump campaign directed them, verify a separate group’s projected deployment total, or report court orders in multiple states.
original_assignment_row.description_long: Reuters reported on disruptions during a July 2024 Wisconsin primary, where activists supporting Trump’s false claims about the 2020 election challenged absentee ballots as workers counted them. Election officials described objections to routine procedures, including how names were read and whether ballot envelopes contained a requested form. Officials said the challenges delayed work and intimidated staff. At least nine observers acted in coordination across three Glendale sites and Milwaukee’s central count, according to local officials. The city’s Democratic mayor said police were called and two observers were ordered to leave after their challenges were found baseless. Reuters also reported that the Republican National Committee and state party trained more than 5,000 observers, while a separate activist group projected up to 1,500 deployments, a number Reuters could not independently verify. The reporting documents local incidents and broader monitoring plans, but it does not establish that Trump personally directed the observers, that their activity occurred across several states, or that courts issued the orders described in the title.
